fiscal_year_end: 31 July (FY2025 = year ended 31 July 2025; half-year balance date 31 January)
overview: KMD Brands is a New Zealand-domiciled, dual-listed (NZX/ASX) multi-brand outdoor and action-sports apparel group operating three brands: Kathmandu (NZ/Australia outdoor retail, founded 1987), Rip Curl (global surf brand acquired October 2019 for ~A$350m) and Oboz (US hiking/outdoor footwear, acquired 2018 for ~US$60m/NZ$83m). The Group designs, sources (predominantly from third-party factories in China, Vietnam, Indonesia and Bangladesh) and sells technical outdoor and surf apparel/footwear through owned retail stores, wholesale/licensed distribution and online, across Australasia, North America, Europe, South America and Asia.

business_model.summary: Vertically-integrated, brand-owned apparel/footwear retailer-wholesaler. Kathmandu is predominantly direct-to-consumer (own retail + online, ~99% of its sales) in AU/NZ and is highly promotional/discount-driven. Rip Curl is a globally diversified wholesale-plus-DTC surf brand (37% wholesale channel per FY25 mix, sold across AU/NZ, North America, Europe, Rest of World). Oboz is almost entirely US wholesale (89% wholesale, 82% USA) supplying outdoor retailers with hiking footwear. Revenue is transactional/seasonal (no subscription or recurring contracts) and working capital is inventory-heavy with pronounced half-year swings tied to Southern Hemisphere winter (Kathmandu) and Northern Hemisphere summer (Rip Curl/Oboz) buying cycles.

revenue_streams.name: Rip Curl
revenue_streams.trend: stable/softening (wholesale growth offset by weaker DTC/same-store sales in 1H FY26)

revenue_streams.name: Kathmandu
revenue_streams.trend: improving/growing (double-digit sales growth in 1H FY26 and into 2H FY26)

revenue_streams.name: Oboz
revenue_streams.trend: recovering off a low base, tariff-pressured

business_model.channel_mix: Group: Retail ~61% (stores), Online ~10%, Wholesale ~28%, Licensing/Royalties ~1% (FY2025). Kathmandu is retail/online-led (~99% DTC); Rip Curl and Oboz skew wholesale.
business_model.geographic_mix: FY2025 Rip Curl: Australia 50%, Europe 19%, North America 24%, Rest of World 12%(approx, multi-region). Kathmandu: Australia 73%, New Zealand 26%. Oboz: USA 82%, Canada 6%, International 12%. Group is AU/NZ-weighted with meaningful North American and European exposure via Rip Curl/Oboz.
business_model.customer_type: B2C (retail/online consumers) plus B2B wholesale accounts (outdoor/surf specialty retailers, department/sporting goods chains) for Rip Curl and Oboz.

competitive_position.market_position: Kathmandu is a top-tier but not dominant outdoor apparel retail brand in AU/NZ, competing directly against Macpac and the vertically-scaled Super Retail Group stable (Anaconda, BCF, Rebel) as well as Decathlon's aggressive value-price entry. Rip Curl is one of the largest global surf brands by revenue (competing with Quiksilver/Billabion/Volcom under Liberated Brands/ABG and Vans) but the action-sports/surf category itself is structurally mature-to-declining in core Western markets. Oboz is a small, sub-scale niche player in US hiking footwear dwarfed by Merrell, Salomon, Hoka and Keen.

moat_factors.description: Rip Curl (est. 1969, Bells Beach) and Kathmandu (est. 1987) have genuine multi-decade brand equity and surf/outdoor authenticity that support wholesale distribution and price realization versus private-label.
Rip Curl's global wholesale footprint (3,900+ doors North America, 1,900+ Europe) took decades to build and is a real, if erodible, distribution asset.
Owned retail network (Kathmandu ~264 AU/NZ stores, Rip Curl ~170 stores) gives full-price and data control, but is also a fixed-cost/lease burden in a promotional category.
Apparel/footwear is a low-switching-cost category; consumers readily substitute between brands based on price and promotion, especially in Kathmandu's heavily discounted AU/NZ market.
KMD is sub-scale versus Super Retail Group, VF Corp, Deckers and Amer Sports on sourcing and marketing spend; it is a price-taker on global apparel manufacturing capacity.

weaknesses: No structural moat in a highly fragmented, low-differentiation apparel/footwear category — this is honestly closer to 'no moat' than a durable competitive advantage
Kathmandu's business model has historically relied on deep promotional discounting to drive traffic, eroding gross margin and training customers to wait for sales
Sub-scale versus larger diversified retail conglomerates (Super Retail Group) and global apparel majors (VF Corp, Deckers, Amer Sports) on sourcing, marketing and digital investment

Two goodwill impairments in three years (Oboz FY2024 $40.3m, Oboz intangibles FY2025 ~$45.4m) evidence that historical M&A (Oboz 2018, Rip Curl 2019) overpaid or has since been impaired by deteriorating trading
High store-network fixed cost base (IFRS 16 lease liabilities) amplifies operating leverage on the downside in a sales downturn

growth_drivers: 'Next Level' three-year turnaround strategy (FY26-FY28): brand/product-led offence, data-driven decision intelligence, and a path to sustainable profitability with targets of ~60% group gross margin and 10% EBITDA margin by FY28
Kathmandu re-acceleration: DTC same-store sales +12.8% in 1H FY26 and +11.1% in the first 6 weeks of 2H FY26, with gross margin expansion from improved product flow/assortment discipline
$27.5m FY26 cost-reset program (on track, ahead of original $25m target) and 21 store closures (15 completed) improving operating leverage toward a <50% opex/sales target
Store network rationalisation and channel/marketplace management (reducing discount marketplace exposure) to lift effective gross margin
New CEO (Brent Scrimshaw, ex-Nike, started March 2025) and new Rip Curl CEO (Ashley Reade, ex-Nike) bringing fresh strategic direction and cost discipline

Balance sheet repair: NZ$65.3m equity raise plus NZ$208m refinanced sustainability-linked debt facility (to Oct-2028) reduces pro forma net debt to ~$32m and leverage to ~1.3x, targeting <0.5x by end FY27

Ongoing full-scale strategic/business review (targeted for completion at FY26 results, 23-Sept-2026) exploring 'non-core asset' options, including divestment of the Southeast Asian (Thailand) wetsuit manufacturing facility (~NZ$5-7m proceeds, ~NZ$6m working capital release)
Rip Curl wholesale strength in Europe and North America partially offsetting weaker DTC/same-store performance
Working capital discipline: inventory at a three-year low, working capital targeted <16% of sales by FY28

business.description: Rip Curl same-store sales fell -2.8% in the 24 weeks to 19-Jul-2026 amid weaker consumer demand and elevated promotional intensity; 1H FY26 Rip Curl underlying EBITDA fell -13.0% YoY despite modest sales growth — the former earnings engine has become a drag.
Kathmandu sales are highly sensitive to Southern Hemisphere winter weather; an unseasonably warm 2026 AU east-coast winter already dented insulated-product sales despite the broader recovery.

Early 1H FY26 momentum is real but the group has a track record of repeated strategic resets (multiple CEOs, cost programs) without sustained margin recovery; FY28 targets (60% GM, 10% EBITDA margin) are still distant.
Competes against far larger, better-capitalised players (Super Retail Group, VF Corp, Deckers, Amer Sports, Decathlon) in categories with weak brand loyalty.
Smallest brand (8% of sales) has been impaired twice; recovery depends on US wholesale demand and tariff mitigation.

financial.description: Leverage reached 3.8x net debt/EBITDA at Jan-2026 (covenant-relevant measure), forcing a covenant reset and a deeply discounted equity raise (NZ$0.06/share, ~69% discount to last traded price, roughly doubling the share count) — existing holders suffered severe dilution.

Extensive owned-store network (Kathmandu ~264 stores AU/NZ, Rip Curl ~170 stores) creates a large lease liability that inflates statutory EBITDA/EBIT volatility and represents a fixed obligation regardless of trading conditions.
Reports in NZD but earns in AUD, USD, EUR and other currencies; FX movements had a ~$9.1m half-year impact on underlying opex and a $5.6m impact on net debt in 1H FY26.

Net working capital peaks materially at January (Northern Hemisphere summer inventory build for Rip Curl, Southern Hemisphere winter build for Kathmandu), creating seasonal net debt peaks (net debt was $94.0m at Jan-2026 vs $52.8m at Jul-2025).
No interim dividend declared in 1H FY26 (or final dividend in FY25) due to operating performance — income investors have no near-term yield support.

regulatory.description: Oboz (82% USA) and Rip Curl US business (~12% of group sales) source heavily from China (35% of branded product spend), Vietnam (31%) and Indonesia (13%); 2025 Trump-era tariffs (up to 54% cumulative on some China-origin goods, 46% Vietnam, 37% Bangladesh) directly hit Oboz gross margin and required inventory rerouting away from the US.
Group sources from ~140+ Tier 1 factories across Asia/South America; reputational and compliance risk typical of the apparel supply chain (modern slavery reporting obligations in NZ/AU).

macro.description: Kathmandu and the Rip Curl Australasia business (50% of Rip Curl sales) are directly exposed to AU/NZ household discretionary spending, which has been weak amid high interest rates/cost-of-living pressure through FY24-FY25.
Elevated promotional intensity across surf/outdoor wholesale channels globally has compressed gross margins group-wide.
Multi-currency revolving debt facilities (~NZ$283m post-refinance) carry floating-rate exposure; higher-for-longer rates increase finance costs on a historically over-levered balance sheet.
Both hemispheres' seasonal weather patterns (mild AU winters hurting Kathmandu insulated-wear, poor surf-season conditions hurting Rip Curl) are an uncontrollable demand swing factor each half.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global outdoor/action-sports apparel is a mature, low-single-digit-growth category in developed markets (management cites the broader 'activity-based' segment growing 5%+, but KMD's core brands have underperformed that backdrop). AU/NZ specialty retail remains structurally challenged by Decathlon's expansion and Super Retail Group's scale.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — consumer discretionary spend, tightly coupled to weather in both hemispheres and to household disposable income cycles in AU/NZ/US/Europe.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high — floating-rate multi-currency revolving debt facility (~NZ$283m post-refinance, reducing toward target as leverage falls); high sensitivity was directly evidenced by the covenant breach pressure and forced recapitalisation in FY26.
key_input_costs: Labour costs at third-party Asian factories

recent_developments.event: Brent Scrimshaw (ex-Nike, ex-Enero Group CEO) appointed Group CEO and Managing Director, replacing Michael Daly who resigned after leading the Group since 2021 and Rip Curl for 22+ years prior.

FY2025 annual result: sales $989.0m (+1% YoY), gross margin fell to 56.5% (-190bps), underlying EBITDA collapsed to $17.7m (from $50.0m FY24), underlying NPAT loss -$28.3m, statutory NPAT loss -$93.6m (vs -$48.3m FY24) driven by a further ~$45.4m Oboz intangible/goodwill impairment; no final dividend declared; announced $25m cost-reset program and 21 store closures.

US tariff announcements (up to ~54% cumulative on China-origin goods, 46% Vietnam, 37% Bangladesh) forced KMD to reroute US-bound inventory to other global markets; estimated ~A$1m FY25 EBITDA impact, larger effect flowing into Oboz FY26 gross margin.

1H FY26 result: sales $505.4m (+7.3% YoY) with growth in both DTC and wholesale; underlying EBITDA more than tripled to $11.5m (from $3.9m); statutory NPAT loss narrowed to -$13.1m (from -$20.7m); Kathmandu DTC same-store sales +12.8%; Rip Curl DTC same-store sales only +1.5%; leverage ratio spiked to 3.8x net debt/EBITDA (covenant measure) forcing action.

Announced NZ$65.3m equity raising (NZ$6.8m placement + NZ$58.5m accelerated renounceable entitlement offer, 1-for-0.73 ratio) at NZ$0.06/share — a 47.1% discount to TERP and 69.2% discount to last traded price — fully underwritten by Goldman Sachs NZ and Forsyth Barr, roughly doubling shares on issue; concurrently refinanced NZ$208m of syndicated, sustainability-linked multi-currency revolving debt facilities extending to 1-October-2028.

KMD Brands commenced a full-scale strategic/business review of its brand portfolio to 'accelerate growth and maximise shareholder value,' explicitly assessing 'non-core assets'; review targeted for completion alongside FY2026 full-year results (23-Sept-2026).

Announced divestment of its Southeast Asian (Thailand) wetsuit manufacturing facility, with production winding down in phases over 12 months; expected to generate ~NZ$5-7m net property proceeds and unlock ~NZ$6m working capital, as part of a shift to a less capital-intensive, DTC-focused model.

Kathmandu DTC same-store sales (incl. online) +4.8%, but Rip Curl same-store sales -2.8% amid weaker consumer demand and increased promotional activity; unseasonably warm AU east-coast winter dented Kathmandu insulated-product sales; FY26 group sales guided to $863.2m-$866.5m (+5% YoY) and underlying EBITDA guided to more than double to $31.5m-$34m.
Ashley Reade (ex-Nike) appointed new CEO of Rip Curl, tasked with reversing the brand's recent same-store-sales decline and repositioning it as the leading global surf brand.

guidance.management_commentary: New CEO Brent Scrimshaw frames FY26 as early proof-points in a 3-year 'Next Level' turnaround built on brand/product-led growth, data-driven decision intelligence and sustainable profitability. Management is explicit that the balance sheet recapitalisation (equity raise + debt refinance) was necessary to fund execution of the strategy and avoid covenant breach, and that a full strategic review of the brand portfolio (including potential divestment of non-core assets) will conclude at the FY2026 results on 23-September-2026 — an outcome investors should treat as a live, unresolved corporate-action risk/catalyst.

bull_case: Balance sheet has just been meaningfully de-risked: pro forma net debt of ~$32m and leverage of 1.3x post the equity raise and NZ$208m debt refinance (to Oct-2028) removes near-term covenant/insolvency risk that was acute as recently as Jan-2026

Kathmandu — the historic problem brand — has genuinely inflected, with DTC same-store sales up double digits for three consecutive trading updates (1H FY26 +12.8%, first 6 weeks 2H +11.1%, 24 weeks to Jul-2026 +4.8% against a warm-winter headwind) alongside gross margin expansion

New management team (CEO Scrimshaw, Rip Curl CEO Reade, both ex-Nike) brings credible operating experience and has already delivered cost savings ahead of target ($27.5m vs $25m) and a leaner store footprint
FY26 guidance implies underlying EBITDA more than doubling ($31.5-34m from $17.7m) with a credible medium-term FY28 roadmap (60% gross margin, 10% EBITDA margin, working capital <16% of sales)

Live strategic/portfolio review concluding at 23-Sept-2026 FY26 results is an explicit value-unlock catalyst — divestment of a brand (or further non-core assets beyond the Thailand facility) could crystallise sum-of-parts value not reflected in the current depressed multiple
Stock trades near/below its heavily discounted (69% to pre-raise price) capital-raise price, arguably offering a low entry point if the turnaround executes
bear_case: Massive, highly dilutive equity raise (NZ$0.06/share, 69.2% discount to last traded price, share count roughly doubled) destroyed substantial per-share value for pre-existing holders and signals the balance sheet was under real distress, not just a precautionary buffer

Rip Curl — formerly the group's profit engine — is now the weak link: same-store sales -2.8% (24 weeks to Jul-2026) and 1H FY26 underlying EBITDA down -13% YoY amid rising promotional intensity, raising the risk that group earnings recovery depends on offsetting a declining core asset with a recovering smaller one (Kathmandu)

Repeated goodwill/intangible impairments (Oboz $40.3m in FY2024, ~$45.4m more in FY2025 — cumulatively wiping out most of the brand's original purchase price) demonstrate a poor M&A track record and raise doubts about the durability of remaining Rip Curl/Oboz carrying values

No structural competitive moat: apparel/footwear retail is low-switching-cost and highly promotional; KMD is sub-scale against Super Retail Group, VF Corp, Deckers and Decathlon, meaning any recovery is vulnerable to being competed away

Multiple unresolved binary risks converge at the 23-Sept-2026 FY26 results/strategic review: outcome of the portfolio review (which brand(s), if any, get divested and at what value), sustainability of Kathmandu's momentum through the seasonally critical winter, and confirmation the FY26 leverage/EBITDA targets are actually met — the current price is arguably pinned to this near-term event rather than steady-state fundamentals
US tariff exposure (Oboz 82% USA, Rip Curl ~12% of group sales from US) remains a live, policy-driven cost headwind with limited company control

corporate_action_flag.description: Two overlapping live/recent corporate actions make the current share price deal-influenced rather than purely fundamentally driven: (1) a NZ$65.3m equity raise (placement + 1-for-0.73 accelerated renounceable entitlement offer) priced at NZ$0.06/share, a 69.2% discount to the pre-announcement last traded price, completed around March-April 2026 and roughly doubling shares on issue — this materially resets any per-share historical comparisons (EPS, DPS, book value per share) at the FY2026H1 mark; and (2) a formal, ongoing strategic/business review explicitly assessing divestment of 'non-core assets' (already resulting in the announced Southeast Asian manufacturing facility sale), due to conclude at the FY2026 full-year results on 23-September-2026 — investors should treat the period through that date as event-driven/deal-pinned, with a material outcome (e.g., a brand divestment announcement) a realistic possibility.
